Montée de l’extrême droite : ces Françai: Rise of the far right: These French people of minority backgrounds in Quebec don't want to go back
Plusieurs Français résidant au Québec co: Several French people living in Quebec share their fears of seeing the far right take power in France, just days before the legislative elections.
De gauche à droite, Sarah Naciri, Leïla: From left to right, Sarah Naciri, Leïla Fayet and Naomie Jiminiga have all three left France for Quebec. They are watching the rise of the far right in their home country with concern. (Illustration: Loubna Chlaikhy)
<strong>31,3% des voix. Le record histor: 31.3% of the vote. The historic record set by the Rassemblement national (RN) in the latest European elections in France, followed by President Macron's decision to dissolve the National Assembly, hit like a political earthquake whose tremors have been felt as far as Quebec. Several French people living here, racialized or queer, share their fears.
La montée de l’extrême droite n’en finit: The rise of the far right in France seems endless. After the presidential party's crushing defeat in the European elections on June 9, 2024, the shock of the announcement that the National Assembly would be dissolved led to a lightning campaign. In Canada, French nationals are called on to vote for their new members of the Assembly on <l1>June 29 and July 6, 2024</l1> (in France, the elections take place on June 30 and July 7).
En quelques jours, une partie des França: In just a few days, part of the French population has gone from shock to fear. Whether they come from immigrant backgrounds, belong to the LGBTQI+ community, or belong to minority religious communities (mainly Muslims and Jews), they all share very concrete worries. Aware that they are the prime targets of the policies advocated by the party of Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella, these French people dread the consequences of the party's hypothetical arrival at Matignon. Traditionally, the president appoints a prime minister from the majority group in the National Assembly.
Au Québec, même si un océan les sépare d: In Quebec, even though an ocean separates them from the Hexagon, racialized French people and those who belong to a marginalized community share the same fears. The number of French people registered with the consular registers of Quebec City and Montréal has nearly doubled since 2005. Despite conditions less favourable than between 1995 and 2002 – a period during which the French were the top group of immigrants to Quebec – between 3,000 and 4,000 of them settle here each year as permanent residents. That number does not include students and holders of temporary permits or working holiday permits, according to the <l1>Consulate General of France in Quebec</l1>.
Nous avons rencontré quatre d’entre elle: We met four of them, all settled in Montréal. They told us about their doubts over a possible return to France, or the reasons why they say their lives are now here.
Sarah Naciri, 21 ans, originaire du Val-: Sarah Naciri, 21, from Val-d'Oise in the Paris suburbs, comes from an Algerian-Moroccan family. Her assertive personality and deep voice give her a maturity that is surprising for her age. After a first university exchange in New Brunswick, Sarah returned to France before coming back to Canada. She settled in Quebec in August 2023 to pursue her postsecondary studies. “In Paris, I was studying at a very elitist university, and the values were the opposite of mine. When I arrived in New Brunswick, I discovered a university system where I finally felt fulfilled. My potential was more recognized there. I told myself, ‘OK, for my master's I absolutely have to leave.’ So I tried my luck and chose Quebec,” she sums up.
Naomie Jiminiga, 19 ans, rayonne naturel: Naomie Jiminiga, 19, is naturally radiant. A wide smile lights up her face when we meet her. Her voice, however, always in tune with her emotions, reveals her sensitivity. The young woman grew up in Normandy, a region in northwestern France that voted strongly for the far right in the European elections of June 9, 2024. Franco-Togolese, Naomi says she grew up in a region with little diversity. “Normandy is very conservative. People are closed-minded. Men are still often seen as superior to women, and the housewife model is still highly valued there.”
C’est en janvier 2023 que Naomie fait le: In January 2023, Naomie took the leap to Quebec to begin university studies in communications. She finds the social contrast striking: “When I arrived, I became aware of the everyday racism I had endured in Normandy and had ended up normalizing!” she exclaims. Despite her new life in la belle province, social media keeps her in touch with her old friends. She did not hesitate to cut that link in the face of “disappointing” remarks from some people around her in the lead-up to the European elections.
« J’ai vu mes amis et des proches publie: “I saw my friends and relatives posting comments like ‘Vote far right!’ Others said ‘We have to kick out the immigrants’ or ‘We have to stop letting these immigrant attackers live in France,’” she says, irritated. “And these are people I know, people I grew up with, you know!”
Leïla Fayet, 56 ans et d'origine franco-: Leïla Fayet, 56, of Franco-Algerian origin, grew up in Lorraine, near Germany, before moving to the south of France and then settling in the Paris region. She has lived in Quebec with her husband and two children for 18 years. It was curiosity about the language that brought them to Quebec in 2006. “We were fascinated by the presence of the French language in the middle of an English-speaking continent,” she says. She and her family also wanted to be closer to nature.
De son côté, Marie, 31 ans, heureuse épo: Marie, 31, happily married to her teenage sweetheart, comes from Bordeaux. She chose Quebec to protect their little boy, born through medically assisted procreation (MAP) carried out in Portugal, from the latent homophobia in France, of which she has too often been a victim. “We went back to France after two years here on a working holiday permit. We got married and had our son, which cost me my relationship with my mother and my brother. I come from the Bordeaux bourgeoisie, which is very attached to institutions like marriage and family, and which did not accept the situation at all,” she says.
Celle qui dirige une agence de voyages s: The woman who runs a travel agency specializing in organizing custom road trips recalls an incident she considers particularly revealing of the intolerance of French society: “Our son spent a year in daycare in Bordeaux, and some parents asked for two children's books to be removed from the library. The first was about a mixed couple, the second about a couple of male storks… It's incredible how far it goes! We held on for a year and then we said, ‘No, enough.’” Marie and her wife therefore chose Quebec and fully intend to build their life here. A decision that recent political events in France only reinforce.
<strong>Record de l’extrême droite aux é: Far-right record in the European elections: “I took it as an insult”
Pour Sarah, Marie, Naomie et Leïla, les: For Sarah, Marie, Naomie and Leïla, the results of the European elections were inevitable. “Honestly, I expected it. The RN has been climbing in the polls for a while now, whether for the European elections, the legislative elections or even the presidential elections. It was predictable,” says Sarah. Leïla, exasperated, makes the same observation: “It's not a surprise, but it's shocking because even when you prepare for it, it's a hell of a blow to take!”
Si elles ne sont pas surprises, elles pe: While they aren't surprised, they see these results as one more rejection, a denial of their French identity. “I grew up in France, and it hurts me to see so many people vote for an openly racist party,” sighs Sarah. “Islamophobia is real in France, and as a Muslim – that's also one of the reasons I came to Canada – when I meet new people, I'm always apprehensive about saying I'm Muslim. People have so many prejudices…” she says.
Naomie, la plus jeune du groupe, partage: Naomie, the youngest of the group, shares the feeling: “I took it as an insult. As a Black woman, even though I'm French, voting for the far right is telling me to leave my own country simply because of my skin colour. For me, the far right is a party driven by hatred. It's not just a desire to ‘expel the attackers,’” she insists.
En remplaçant le stigmate de la couleur: Replacing the stigma of skin colour with that of sexual orientation, Marie describes the same feeling of rejection. “I'm a woman, I'm a lesbian and I have a child. It's exactly the same pattern as racism, I'm one of the first people concerned… In the moment, I felt like everyone in my country was against me, actually. These are no longer isolated cases.” With 93% of municipalities putting the far right in first place, the French discovered a map covered in navy blue when the results of the European elections were revealed on June 9.
Carte présentant les résultats des élect: Map showing the results of the 2024 European elections in France. (Infographic: data.gouv.fr)
Au fil des dernières années, elle assure: Over the past few years, she says, she has felt the country tipping over, the last barriers falling, and hateful remarks and acts becoming more and more common, including in public. “At Bordeaux Pride in 2020, we were attacked by extremists, guys who climbed up onto the quays to throw smoke bombs at us,” she says indignantly. “Same thing at Paris Pride! We left two and a half hours late because the far right was blocking the march. After that, I started to feel unsafe.”
Malgré tout, ces cinq Montréalaises d’ad: Despite everything, these five adopted Montrealers, who fully intend to use their right to vote starting June 29, are making an effort to understand what is driving some of their fellow citizens toward the RN.
<strong>Chômage, inflation, dégradation: Unemployment, inflation, deteriorating public services… the anger of the French
Selon ces femmes interrogées, la montée: According to these women, the rise of the far right is partly due to a widespread weariness with traditional politics. Sarah, who holds a bachelor's degree in political science from Panthéon-Assas University in Paris, explains: “I feel like it's inevitable. People are fed up with the current system, which is running out of steam. Populists promise change and, unfortunately, it's often the far right. That's who people vote for, because they see that the system is stuck and they want to reform it.”
« C'est peut-être aussi un moyen pour le: “Maybe it's also a way for French people to say, ‘Well, maybe I'm not racist, maybe I don't buy into those ideas, but I want to shock. I'm sick of it. So I'm voting RN.’ And it works. It's a way of shocking, of saying we want change at any cost,” says Sarah. Naomie agrees: “I feel like everyone is fed up with living conditions in France, so we leave the field open to those who already support the far right. There was still a lot of abstention.”
Lors des dernières élections européennes: In the latest European elections, France recorded an abstention rate of 48.51%. The country's economic and social context, with an unemployment rate of 7.5%, is said to be a key factor in understanding the seemingly unstoppable rise of the RN vote.
Leïla fait d'ailleurs une comparaison fr: Leïla also makes a striking comparison: “I was talking with a Jewish friend who lived through the Second World War, and she was sharing her worries with me. She feels there is an atmosphere in France right now similar to ’39–’45, not in terms of Nazis. Not that. But in terms of disinformation, suspicion, poverty, with the discourse of ‘I don't like you, you, the other.’ Then the rise of the far right,” she recalls.
Sarah, qui parle avec les mains, accuse: Sarah, who talks with her hands, blames the RN's demagogic rhetoric: “There are surely women who consider themselves feminists and who voted for Jordan Bardella because they didn't do their research. The French heard Jordan Bardella say: fine, we're going to get rid of all the Arabs and Black people in France. They told themselves, ‘OK, immigration will fix everything: let's go.’ And they don't look any further. Unfortunately, the Rassemblement national is winning people over through this rhetoric.”
Naomie est du même avis. « Imagine, comm: Naomie shares this view. “Imagine,” she begins, with a stoic gaze, “if every day you hear that your children aren't safe because immigrants kill; because immigrants are attackers; and that if you're poor it's because too much money is given to immigrants…” She pauses, then continues in a dismayed tone: “The French are bound to go after immigrants because they think they've found the solution to their problem.”
Ces femmes voient donc dans le soutien à: These women therefore see support for the far right as an expression of a desire for change and of frustration with a system perceived as stagnant. But they fear what would happen if the far right were to reach Matignon.
<strong>« La France a vraiment un problè: “France really has a problem to fix before I go back”
Si chaque expatriation est unique, les F: While every expatriation is unique, many French people leave in search of a better quality of life, professional opportunities they don't always have in their own country, better pay… But many go back to France after a few years. Missing loved ones, disillusionment with the Quebec health care system for some, or the existence of a very real xenophobia, even if it is not expressed in the same way, are among the reasons for these early returns.
L’éventuelle accession du RN au pouvoir: Could the RN's possible rise to power within a month, or in the next presidential election scheduled for 2027, change the equation? When asked whether they would consider going back to France one day, Naomie and Marie answer with a categorical no.
« J’ai très peur de ce qui va se passer: “I'm very afraid of what will happen to the queer community if we tip to the far right! In Italy, when Giorgia Meloni took power, she took the birth certificates of kids who were born through MAP and removed [from those certificates] all the mothers who hadn't carried the child. In my case, I could lose all parental rights to my son, since it's my wife who carried him. It's horrible!” Marie says heatedly. The RN did in fact vote against the Taubira law legalizing “marriage for all,” which was ultimately adopted by a relatively slim majority.
Partie pour profiter de sa vie de famill: Having left to enjoy her family life more freely, she has no plans to return to France. “I'd rather stay here. We want a second child, and it's easier here! We won't have any problems, we won't have to fight. I'm 31, I've been through a lot of complicated things, and now I just want a normal life where people accept us without us having to fight for everything,” she explains.
« Quand je suis arrivée au Canada, j'ava: “When I arrived in Canada, I was nostalgic for France. But the more I compare Canada's evolution with France's, the more I tell myself France really has a problem to fix before I go back,” says Naomie, shaking her head. “Here, I feel safe, whereas in France I was confronted with racist people and insults simply because I'm a woman. I don't want to go back to my own country; it's almost dangerous. It's serious.”
Leïla et Sarah sont plus tiraillées. Apr: Leïla and Sarah are more torn. After a brief moment of reflection, Leïla recalls several painful experiences: “I've lived in several regions of France and I often ran into extremists. You really risk your life facing them. It's simple. You can be physically attacked.” She adds firmly: “If I didn't have children and the far right came to power, I'd go back there to resist. But with children, I prefer to stay here.”
Sarah, la dernière à être arrivée au Qué: Sarah, the last to arrive in Quebec, last August, expresses ambivalent feelings: “The more time passes, the more I ask myself the question. I miss my loved ones enormously, but the comfort I have here is incomparable, and it's hard to see myself going back to France to face a wave of racism and Islamophobia.”
Si ces Françaises perçoivent souvent le: While these Frenchwomen often see Quebec as a less racist society that is more tolerant toward minorities, that perception needs to be put in perspective. Quebec society is indeed not free of a certain xenophobia, even if it tends to express it less openly. “Systemic racism exists in Quebec. However, despite the many reports and events that attest to its presence, the government still refuses to acknowledge it and to intervene in response to this injustice,” observes Amnestie Internationale Canada Francophone, which is behind an <l1>email campaign</l1> to call on political leaders.
En 2020, quelques temps après le meurtre: In 2020, some time after the murder of George Floyd by a police officer in the United States, the Quebec government committed to a policy of fighting racism while rejecting the notion of “systemic racism.” The Groupe d'action contre le racisme was created in its wake and published a report titled <l1>“Le racisme au Québec : tolérance zéro”</l1> in December of that year. It lists several “strong measures for a society without racism,” as well as “convincing actions to respond to Indigenous realities.”
Quatre ans plus tard, les discrimination: Four years later, racial discrimination in access to employment or housing, discriminatory policing and the erasure of Indigenous identity are still very much current. “Concretely, among visible minorities living in Quebec, 32.1% say they have experienced racial discrimination in their job search,” according to the survey on the individual trajectories and dynamics of participation of women and men in Quebec society <l1>(TraJIpaQ, 2020)</l1>. This discrimination varies according to people's origin and immigration status.
L’Observatoire des inégalités raciales a: The Observatoire des inégalités raciales au Québec, a body created in 2021, also notes in <l1>a bulletin</l1> that: “religious symbols, notably the wearing of the veil, are characteristic of the experience of racism in hiring in Quebec. In this regard, among African women who reported experiencing racial discrimination in employment (31%), 85% are Maghrebi and wear the veil.”
Les discriminations liées au genre ou à: Discrimination based on gender or sexual orientation is also commonplace. “With equal qualifications, women face notable discrimination, with an average hourly wage lower than that of men,” notes the Observatoire québécois des inégalités raciales au Québec.
Enfin, dès 2021, le Centre d'expertise e: Finally, as early as 2021, the Centre d'expertise et de formation sur les intégrismes religieux, les idéologies politiques et la radicalisation (CEFIR) noted that Quebec is not immune to the rise of the far right seen since the early 2010s. “Not only has the Quebec far right seen a staggering increase in its activities during this period (6,350%), but (...) these increasingly involve violence (verbal, physical and cyberviolence),” the CEFIR states in <l1>a study published in May 2024</l1>.
Sur le plan politique, l’extrême droite: On the political front, the far right long remained very marginal. But the context is changing quickly. “On the Quebec side, the reasonable accommodation crisis (2007) had a notable impact on public opinion and on nationalist political forces (the Parti québécois and the Coalition avenir Québec), gradually leading them to support an identity-based, moderate and opportunistic nationalism,” points out researcher Maxim Fortin in an article published in À Bâbord - Revue sociale et politique. As in France, the far right's demagogic rhetoric targets immigration, particularly Muslims, and “takes an interest in Indigenous peoples in the hope of drawing them into a struggle alongside ‘old-stock Québécois’ against ‘foreigners,’” according to the researcher.
Si le Québec semble marcher dans les pas: While Quebec seems to be following in the footsteps of its cousin across the Atlantic, in France nothing is settled yet. We will have to wait for the second round of the legislative elections, which ends on the evening of Sunday, July 7, to find out whether France's history will tip toward the far right or whether it will get a new reprieve… until the next elections.
